summary:
Mars could be humanity's next home. But before we build a civilization, we need to answer one critical question: Where do we begin?

That's where Conquering Mars comes in.

We developed an interactive, data-driven platform that transforms complex NASA planetary data into meaningful insights, helping humanity explore and evaluate potential settlement locations on Mars.

Instead of navigating complicated scientific datasets, users can explore Martian regions, compare candidate sites, assess terrain suitability, and plan exploration routes. Our uncertainty-aware route comparison helps users evaluate different paths while understanding the scientific evidence, terrain challenges, and confidence behind each assessment.

Built using NASA's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) terrain data and Microsoft Azure, our platform bridges planetary science and modern technology, making complex information accessible without overlooking scientific uncertainty.

Our goal is to transform planetary data into actionable insights, empowering future researchers, engineers, and explorers to make more informed decisions about humanity's future beyond Earth.

Because the first step toward living on Mars isn't just getting there. It's knowing where to begin.
details:
Conquering Mars - Turning Martian Data Into Exploration Decisions

The Challenge: Where Do We Begin?

Imagine planning a future crewed traverse across the Martian surface.

Two routes are available. One looks preferable under normal terrain assumptions. The other becomes more attractive when uncertainty in the terrain is considered.

Which would you choose? And more importantly, what would you need to know before making that decision?

Mars could become humanity's next home. But before we establish infrastructure or send humans across unfamiliar landscapes, we need more than maps. We need tools that help us understand terrain, evaluate alternatives, and recognize uncertainty.

NASA has already collected remarkable planetary data. Our challenge was to transform that information into an accessible, interactive exploration experience.

Our Solution: More Than a Map

Conquering Mars is a cloud-powered, 3D exploration and planning platform built around real NASA scientific data.

Our application focuses on a 4 × 8 km study area in Deuteronilus Mensae, a Martian region characterized by complex terrain and evidence of past glacial activity.

Through our interactive platform, users can:

  • Explore Mars in 3D: Navigate real Martian terrain derived from NASA imagery and elevation measurements.
  • Evaluate Potential Infrastructure: Compare candidate zones for habitats, landing sites, greenhouses, data centers, solar installations, and potential ice access.
  • Compare Exploration Routes: Investigate how different terrain assumptions influence route selection.
  • Identify Scouting Priorities: Discover locations where additional investigation could reduce uncertainty.
  • Understand the Science: Examine terrain conditions, modeling assumptions, and limitations behind planning results.

Rather than simply presenting locations, our platform helps users explore why one planning option may be preferable to another.

Our Key Innovation: Planning With Uncertainty

Finding a route is one challenge. Understanding how uncertainty changes that route is another.

Conquering Mars compares two routes generated using the A* pathfinding algorithm:

  1. Standard Route: Uses nominal terrain traversability to identify a preferred path based on the modeled terrain conditions.
  2. Uncertainty-Aware Route: Adds penalties for terrain sensitive to modeled slope uncertainty, revealing how different assumptions can change route selection.

By comparing both approaches, users can investigate tradeoffs between route distance and modeled terrain exposure.

Our platform also identifies scout locations along the standard route where nominal and uncertainty-adjusted traversability differ significantly. These markers highlight areas where further investigation could be particularly valuable.

This introduces a question that goes beyond conventional route optimization:

"What do we need to learn before deciding?"

Conquering Mars brings terrain visualization, route comparison, and investigation priorities into one experience, making modeled uncertainty visible alongside exploration planning.

The Technology Behind Conquering Mars

Our platform combines planetary science, computational modeling, interactive 3D visualization, and cloud engineering.

  • NASA HiRISE Data: We use a stereo-derived digital terrain model from NASA's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment to analyze Martian elevation and terrain characteristics.
  • Python: Powers scientific data processing, terrain analysis, and our backend API.
  • A Pathfinding:* Generates baseline and uncertainty-aware routes using different terrain-cost assumptions.
  • React and TypeScript: Power our interactive user interface.
  • Three.js: Renders the Martian landscape as an explorable 3D environment.
  • Microsoft Azure: Azure Static Web Apps and Azure Functions host our application and make the experience publicly accessible.

To balance performance and analytical precision, we use a downsampled terrain mesh for interactive visualization while retaining the underlying scientific grid for point measurements.

Within the hackathon's limited development window, our team integrated these components into a working end-to-end prototype.

Open-Source Code and Technical Documentation

Our project is publicly available on GitHub, allowing judges to explore the source code, scientific methodology, terrain-processing pipeline, route-planning algorithms, and application architecture.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/isa9955/NASA-Space-Apps-2026

By making our work accessible, we aim to encourage transparency, reproducibility, and further exploration of planetary science through software engineering.

Scientific Integrity: Understanding What We Don't Know

Good science isn't just about finding answers. It's about knowing how much confidence we can place in them.

Scientific validity and transparency were central to our approach.

Rather than attempting to evaluate the entire Martian surface, we concentrated on a defined study area where we could apply reproducible terrain analysis.

Our uncertainty model measures sensitivity to terrain assumptions. It does not provide calibrated probabilities of mission safety.

Likewise, our infrastructure assessments are preliminary terrain-based comparisons, not certified construction recommendations.

Several important limitations remain:

  • Local ice availability has not been confirmed. Our preliminary ice-access assessment relies on a draft landform interpretation rather than direct resource measurements.
  • A known threshold inconsistency currently limits interpretation of the solar-zone comparison.
  • Radiation exposure, confirmed water accessibility, and other environmental hazards require additional scientific investigation.

These limitations are important because terrain suitability alone cannot establish whether a location is safe or habitable for humans.

By surfacing assumptions and uncertainty alongside planning results, we aim to make the exploration process more scientifically responsible.

Our Impact: From Planetary Data to Better Decisions

Conquering Mars demonstrates how NASA's publicly available scientific data can become an accessible tool for education, exploration, and preliminary engineering analysis.

For students, it makes planetary science interactive and understandable. For researchers, it demonstrates ways to communicate complex terrain information and uncertainty. For future engineers and mission planners, it offers a prototype for evaluating planning alternatives and identifying where further observations might be useful.

Our vision is to expand this approach with additional scientific datasets, more sophisticated environmental models, and rigorous validation to support broader planetary exploration research.

We are not claiming to have discovered the perfect location for humanity's first Martian settlement.

We are demonstrating how science and technology can help us explore possibilities, understand tradeoffs, and identify what needs to be investigated next.

Because the first step toward living on Mars isn't simply getting there.

It's knowing where to begin, understanding the challenges along the way, and asking the right questions before taking the next step.
